clinicalPearls: Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a thermal dimorphic fungus; H. capsulatum var. capsulatum predominates in North America, while var. duboisii in Africa produces larger yeasts and a clinically distinct disease with frequent skin and bone involvement (p.1692-1693, 1695).

Most prevalent endemic mycosis in North America, classically the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, with foci in Mexico, Central/South America (Brazil), Africa and Asia; soil enriched with bird or bat droppings promotes growth, and disruption aerosolizes microconidia (p.1693).
High-exposure, high-attack-rate activities include spelunking (cave exposure), excavation, cleaning chicken coops, demolition/remodeling of old buildings and cutting dead trees (p.1693).
Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic infection to life-threatening illness; severity depends on intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1694).

Acute pulmonary disease appears 1-4 weeks after exposure as a flulike illness (fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, anorexia, dry cough, dyspnea, chest pain), often with hilar/mediastinal adenopathy on chest radiograph (p.1694).
Arthralgia/arthritis with erythema nodosum occurs in 5-10% of acute cases and represents an inflammatory response, not extrapulmonary spread; pericarditis may also develop (p.1694).

Chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis occurs in smokers with structural lung disease (e.g., bullous emphysema), with productive cough, dyspnea, low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates resembling tuberculosis (p.1694).

Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) involves the reticuloendothelial system - lungs, bone marrow, spleen, liver, adrenal glands and mucocutaneous membranes; common findings are fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia, with possible meningitis, oral/GI ulceration and adrenal insufficiency (p.1694).
Fungal culture is the diagnostic gold standard but may take up to 1 month and is often negative in less severe cases; in PDH yield is highest from BAL fluid, bone marrow aspirate and blood (p.1694).

Detection of Histoplasma antigen in body fluids is extremely useful for PDH and acute diffuse pulmonary disease (sensitivity >95% in PDH, >80% in severe acute pulmonary disease when both urine and serum are tested); urine is often positive in disseminated disease (p.1694-1695, 1693).
Antigen levels correlate with severity in PDH, fall with effective therapy, and a stable or rising level predicts relapse or treatment failure (p.1695-1696).

Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation, IgG/IgM EIA) is especially useful in immunocompetent patients and for chronic pulmonary disease; IgM appears first and declines, IgG appears later and rises (p.1695).
harrison.pathophysiology: Infection follows inhalation of microconidia, the naturally infectious mycelial form; particles 2-4 micrometers reach terminal bronchioles and alveoli where alveolar macrophages engulf them and they transform into small (2-5 micrometer) narrow-budding yeasts, a calcium- and iron-dependent process central to pathogenesis. Yeasts evade the immune system and multiply within resting macrophages, then translocate via phagosomes to draining lymph nodes and spread hematogenously throughout the reticuloendothelial system. Effective cellular immunity develops about 2 weeks after infection, with T-cell interferon-gamma helping macrophages kill the organism; IL-12 and TNF-alpha are essential to cellular immunity. In immunocompetent hosts, organized granulomas contain the organisms and typically fibrose and calcify (calcified lung nodules, mediastinal nodes, hepatosplenic calcifications), and infection confers protective immunity to reinfection. With impaired cellular immunity, infection is not contained and disseminates as progressive disseminated histoplasmosis. Structural lung disease such as emphysema impairs clearance and leads to chronic pulmonary disease with progressive inflammation, necrosis and fibrosis mimicking cavitary tuberculosis (p.1693-1694).
additionalDifferentials: Primary or metastatic lung cancer (asymptomatic pulmonary nodules)
Other endemic/dimorphic mycoses: blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis
infectionMimics: Cavitary tuberculosis (chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis mimics this radiographically and pathologically)
nonInfectiousMimics: Primary lung cancer (asymptomatic controlled nodules found on screening CT in smokers)
additionalInvestigations: Histoplasma antigen detection in urine and serum (and BAL fluid; CSF for CNS disease)
Lateral flow antigen point-of-care testing for resource-limited settings
Histoplasma serology: immunodiffusion (ID), complement fixation (CF), IgG and IgM enzyme immunoassay (EIA)
Fungal culture (BAL fluid, sputum/bronchial washings, blood, bone marrow aspirate; positive in ~75% of PDH and chronic pulmonary disease)
Fungal stains/cytopathology or biopsy of affected organ (BAL fluid, bone marrow, liver, adrenal) showing small narrow-budding intracellular yeasts
Chest radiograph/CT (pneumonitis, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, upper-lobe cavitation, calcified nodes)
Workup for rare genetic immunodeficiencies of the IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha pathways in healthy individuals presenting with PDH
redFlags: Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH), typically in immunocompromised hosts (~70% of cases), especially AIDS with CD4+ count <200/microliter
Acute rapidly fatal PDH with diffuse interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates, respiratory failure, shock, coagulopathy and multiorgan failure
Onset of PDH while on anti-TNF-alpha therapy, methotrexate or other biologic/immunosuppressive agents, or post-transplant immunosuppression
CNS involvement: meningitis or focal brain lesions
Fibrosing mediastinitis causing superior vena cava syndrome, pulmonary vessel obstruction or airway obstruction (fatal in up to one-third of cases)
Large mediastinal masses compressing great vessels, airways or esophagus, or rupturing to form fistulae (e.g., bronchoesophageal)
harrison.prognosis: Most immunocompetent individuals with low-level exposure are asymptomatic or have a mild, self-limited illness that resolves without therapy; up to 75% of adults in endemic areas have evidence of prior infection without clinical disease. Untreated chronic cavitary disease is slowly progressive. Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis ranges from an acute, rapidly fatal course to a subacute/chronic one and is a devastating illness requiring prompt recognition, particularly in AIDS or anti-TNF therapy. Fibrosing mediastinitis is fatal in up to one-third of cases. Antigen levels track severity and response, with stable or rising levels signaling treatment failure or relapse (p.1693-1696).
pitfalls: Chronic cavitary histoplasmosis closely mimics cavitary tuberculosis radiographically (upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, pleural thickening) and may be misdiagnosed as TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma or malignancy.
Asymptomatic calcified nodules from controlled prior infection may be mistaken for malignancy on screening CT in smokers from endemic areas.
Fungal stains may misidentify staining artifacts or other fungal elements as Histoplasma yeasts.
Persistent antibodies for several years after infection can cause a false misdiagnosis of active histoplasmosis in a patient with another disease process.
ID and CF serology are insensitive early in infection and have reduced sensitivity in immunosuppressed patients, especially organ transplant recipients.
Antigen testing cross-reacts with African histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis and rarely aspergillosis.
Fibrosing mediastinitis is a chronic fibrotic reaction to past infection, not active disease, and does NOT respond to antifungal therapy.
Unlike latent tuberculosis, inactive histoplasmosis does NOT reactivate.
harrison.severityClassification: Clinical forms (Harrison Table 218-1): acute pulmonary, mild to moderate; acute pulmonary, severe with respiratory failure (ARDS); chronic/cavitary pulmonary; progressive disseminated (PDH); and central nervous system disease. Severity is graded by intensity of exposure, host immune status and underlying lung architecture (p.1693-1695).
management: Observation without antifungals for mild, self-limited acute pulmonary disease in immunocompetent hosts
Azole antifungal (itraconazole) for mild-to-moderate disease and as step-down consolidation therapy
Liposomal amphotericin B for severe or progressive disseminated disease, followed by itraconazole
Corticosteroids as an adjunct in severe respiratory compromise or inflammatory complications
In HIV and other immunocompromised patients, antiretroviral therapy, treatment of the acute infection, and prolonged azole suppression as secondary prophylaxis
Monitor serum and urine Histoplasma antigen to gauge treatment response and detect relapse
Manage complications such as pericarditis and fibrosing mediastinitis, and reduce high-risk environmental exposure
